title: Catching NumberFormatException (Unchecked)
description: Write a method parseIntSafely(String s) that attempts to parse a string as an integer and returns the integer on success, or -1 if the string is not a valid number. Test with valid and invalid inputs.
hints: Wrap Integer.parseInt(s) in a try-catch(NumberFormatException e).
NumberFormatException is unchecked (extends RuntimeException) — no throws declaration needed.

solution.explanation: NumberFormatException is an unchecked exception (it extends RuntimeException) — the compiler does not require you to catch it or declare it with throws. Unchecked exceptions represent programming errors or invalid inputs that the programmer may or may not choose to handle. Checked exceptions (like IOException) must be either caught or declared; they represent conditions the caller should reasonably handle. Here, wrapping the parse in a try-catch makes the method recover gracefully from bad input, returning a sentinel value (-1) that the caller can check. Printing e.getMessage() is useful for debugging but in production you'd log the exception properly.

methodSignatures.description: Parses the string as a signed decimal integer; throws NumberFormatException if the string is not a valid integer.

title: Catching IOException (Checked Exception)
description: Write a method readFirstLine(String path) that reads and returns the first line of a text file using BufferedReader, or null if the file doesn't exist. The method must handle the checked IOException.
hints: IOException is a checked exception — you must catch it or declare throws IOException.
Catching inside the method is cleaner if callers don't need to know about the file operation.

solution.explanation: IOException is a checked exception — any method that might throw it must either catch it (as we do here) or declare throws IOException in its signature. Checked exceptions model recoverable conditions: a missing file is something the program can meaningfully react to. The trade-off of catching inside the method is that callers don't need to know about the IO detail, but they lose the ability to distinguish 'file not found' from 'permission denied' (both return null). Note this code has a resource-leak bug if readLine() throws — the reader won't be closed; try-with-resources (exercise exceptions-004) is the proper fix.

methodSignatures.description: Reads a line of text, returning null at end of stream; throws IOException on error.

title: Multi-Catch: Catching Multiple Exception Types
description: Write a method processInput(String s) that: (1) parses s as an integer, (2) looks up an element in an array at that index. Use a single catch block (multi-catch) to handle both NumberFormatException and ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. Also show catch ordering (specific before general).
hints: Multi-catch syntax: catch (NumberFormatException | ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException e)
The exception variable in a multi-catch is implicitly final — you cannot reassign it.

solution.explanation: Multi-catch (added in Java 7) allows a single catch block to handle multiple exception types using the | operator, avoiding duplicate handler code when the recovery logic is the same for all caught types. The exception variable is implicitly final in a multi-catch block to prevent type confusion. Catch blocks must be ordered from most specific to most general — if you put catch(Exception e) before catch(NumberFormatException e), the compiler rejects it because the more specific type is unreachable. This specific-before-general rule mirrors class hierarchy: NumberFormatException extends IllegalArgumentException extends RuntimeException extends Exception.

methodSignatures.description: Returns the detail message string describing this throwable.
Returns the simple name of the underlying class (without package).

title: finally: Guaranteed Cleanup
description: Demonstrate that a finally block runs even when: (1) the try block completes normally, (2) the try block throws an exception, (3) the try block executes a return statement. Show that finally always executes before the method returns.
hints: finally runs before the method returns even when return is inside the try block.
If finally also has a return, it overrides the return value from the try block.

solution.explanation: The finally block is guaranteed to execute after the try (and any matching catch) block, regardless of whether an exception occurred or whether a return statement was hit. This makes it the right place to release resources (close files, database connections) that must be freed no matter what happens. When the try block has a return statement, finally still executes before the value is actually returned to the caller. Critically, if the finally block itself contains a return, it overrides any return value from the try block — this is considered a bad practice because it can silently discard exceptions or change return values unexpectedly.

title: Try-With-Resources: AutoCloseable
description: Create a custom AutoCloseable resource class that prints a message when closed. Use try-with-resources to auto-close it. Then open two resources in a single try-with-resources block and observe the closing order. Demonstrate that the resource is closed even when an exception is thrown.
hints: @Override public void close() { System.out.println("Closed: " + name); }
Multiple resources: try (R1 r1 = ...; R2 r2 = ...) — they close in reverse order (r2 first).

solution.explanation: Try-with-resources (Java 7+) automatically calls close() on any resource that implements AutoCloseable at the end of the try block, whether it exits normally or via an exception. This eliminates the need for a finally block to close resources and prevents resource leaks when exceptions occur mid-way. When multiple resources are declared, they are closed in the reverse order of declaration (LIFO) — this mirrors the natural stack unwinding order and ensures resources that depend on others are closed first. The close() call happens before any catch block executes, which is important for flushing buffers before handling errors.

methodSignatures.description: Closes this resource, relinquishing any underlying resources. Called automatically by try-with-resources.

title: Suppressed Exceptions in Try-With-Resources
description: Create a resource whose close() method itself throws an exception. Demonstrate that when both the try body and close() throw, the body's exception is the primary exception and close()'s exception is added as a suppressed exception. Access it with getSuppressed().
hints: The primary exception (from the try body) propagates; close()'s exception is suppressed.
Use e.getSuppressed() to retrieve the suppressed exceptions array.

solution.explanation: Before try-with-resources, if both the try body and a finally block threw exceptions, the body's exception was silently swallowed by the finally exception — a notorious source of hard-to-diagnose bugs. Try-with-resources solves this: if both the body and close() throw, the body's exception is the primary exception that propagates, and close()'s exception is attached as a 'suppressed' exception accessible via getSuppressed(). This preserves the original exception while still giving you access to the cleanup failure. getSuppressed() returns an array because multiple resources might each throw on close(), each becoming a separate suppressed exception.

methodSignatures.description: Returns an array of all exceptions that were suppressed in order to deliver this exception.
Appends the specified exception to the exceptions that were suppressed in order to deliver this exception.

title: Custom Checked Exception
description: Create a custom checked exception InsufficientFundsException (extends Exception) with fields amount and balance. Use it in a BankAccount class whose withdraw method throws it. The exception should have a constructor that takes both values and builds a descriptive message.
hints: class InsufficientFundsException extends Exception — it's checked, so callers must handle it.
Pass a descriptive message to super() in the constructor.

solution.explanation: Extending Exception (not RuntimeException) makes the exception checked — the compiler forces any caller of withdraw() to either catch InsufficientFundsException or declare throws InsufficientFundsException. This is appropriate here because insufficient funds is a foreseeable, recoverable business condition that callers should explicitly handle. Adding domain-specific fields (amount, balance) with getters enriches the exception with structured data beyond the message string — the catch block can access these to present accurate feedback or make decisions programmatically without parsing the message string. Calling super(message) ensures the message is stored in the standard Throwable.getMessage() location.

methodSignatures.description: Constructs a new exception with the specified detail message.
Returns the detail message string of this throwable.

title: Custom Unchecked Exception with Cause
description: Create an unchecked exception DatabaseException (extends RuntimeException) that wraps a low-level cause. Create a UserRepository that catches low-level exceptions (like NullPointerException for a simulated DB error) and wraps them in DatabaseException. Demonstrate getCause().
hints: RuntimeException has constructors: (String msg), (String msg, Throwable cause), (Throwable cause).
getCause() returns the original Throwable that was wrapped.

solution.explanation: Extending RuntimeException makes DatabaseException unchecked — callers are not forced to declare or catch it, which is appropriate for unexpected technical failures where there's often nothing useful to do at the call site (the operation fundamentally can't complete). Exception wrapping (chaining) is critical for abstraction: the repository's contract is about users, not SQL drivers or network connections — callers shouldn't need to handle JDBC-specific exceptions. Passing the original exception as the cause preserves the full stack trace and the root cause, which is invaluable when debugging. Never swallow the cause by creating new DatabaseException(message) without passing e.

methodSignatures.description: Constructs a RuntimeException with the specified detail message and cause.
Returns the cause of this throwable, or null if the cause is nonexistent or unknown.

title: Exception Chaining and Re-Throwing with Cause
description: Build a three-layer architecture: DAO -> Service -> Controller. Each layer catches exceptions from the layer below and wraps them in its own exception type, preserving the cause. Show the full exception chain by printing each exception and its cause.
hints: Each layer: catch(LowerException e) { throw new UpperException("msg", e); }
Traverse the chain with t.getCause() until null.

solution.explanation: Exception chaining builds a causal chain that maps exactly to architectural boundaries: the ControllerException at the top is what the HTTP layer deals with, ServiceException is what business logic deals with, DataAccessException is what persistence deals with, and the root RuntimeException is the raw technical failure. Each layer translates the vocabulary of its concern without discarding lower-level context. getCause() lets you traverse the chain programmatically to find the root cause; Throwable also has printStackTrace() which prints the full chained trace automatically. This pattern is essential for production observability — without it, a 'request handling failed' error tells you nothing about whether it was a DB timeout, network error, or coding bug.

methodSignatures.description: Returns the cause of this throwable, or null if none.
Prints this throwable and its backtrace, including the cause chain, to standard error.

title: Don't Swallow Exceptions — Log and Rethrow
description: Demonstrate three anti-patterns: (1) catching Exception blindly, (2) empty catch blocks (swallowing), (3) losing the cause. Then demonstrate the correct pattern: catch specifically, log with context, and rethrow with cause.
hints: An empty catch block hides the error completely — a bug becomes invisible.
Log the context (what was being processed) and wrap with the original cause.

solution.explanation: Catching Exception (or Throwable) is an anti-pattern because it also catches programming errors (NullPointerException, ClassCastException) that should crash the program to surface bugs early. Empty catch blocks are even worse — they silently discard exceptions, making failures invisible and leaving the program in an inconsistent state. Dropping the cause when rethrowing (new MyException(msg) without passing e) destroys the stack trace of the original error, making root-cause analysis impossible. The correct pattern is: catch the most specific exception type you can handle, log enough context to reproduce the problem, and rethrow with the original exception as the cause to preserve the full diagnostic chain.

methodSignatures.description: Constructs an IllegalArgumentException with the specified message and cause.

title: Exception-Safe Resource Handling Without Try-With-Resources
description: Before Java 7, resource cleanup required careful finally block patterns. Implement a method that opens two resources and must ensure both are closed even if an exception occurs during processing — correctly using the nested try-finally pattern. Then compare to the try-with-resources version.
hints: Old way: initialize to null, open in try, close in finally (null-check first).
Nested try-finally for two resources: outer opens first, inner opens second.

solution.explanation: The old-style pattern initializes resources to null before the try block, opens them inside the try, then in the finally block null-checks and closes them in reverse order — each close is individually wrapped in its own try-catch so that a failure to close one resource doesn't prevent closing the other. This pattern is correct but verbose, and it's very easy to get wrong (forget the null check, wrong close order, forget to wrap close in try-catch). Try-with-resources produces identical behavior with a fraction of the code, handles close exceptions as suppressed exceptions automatically, and is impossible to get wrong. Use try-with-resources for all new code.

title: Custom Exception Hierarchy for a Domain
description: Design a small exception hierarchy for an e-commerce order system: OrderException (base, checked), PaymentException (extends OrderException), InventoryException (extends OrderException). Create an OrderService that may throw any of these. Catch them at different levels of specificity.
hints: PaymentException extends OrderException, which extends Exception.
Catch OrderException to handle all order errors; catch PaymentException for payment-specific handling.

solution.explanation: A well-designed exception hierarchy lets callers choose their level of handling granularity. Catching PaymentException allows payment-specific recovery (retry with a different card); catching the parent OrderException handles any order problem generically (show a user-friendly error page). The hierarchy must be declared from most specific to most general in catch blocks — since PaymentException is a subtype of OrderException, it must appear first. Each subclass carries domain-specific fields (amount, item, requested) rather than forcing callers to parse the message string. Making OrderException checked (extends Exception) forces callers to acknowledge that placing an order can fail, which is appropriate for a business operation with known failure modes.

methodSignatures.description: Constructs a new exception with the specified detail message.
Constructs a new exception with the specified detail message and cause.

title: throws Declaration and Checked Exception Propagation
description: Demonstrate the throws keyword: write a call chain methodA() -> methodB() -> methodC() where methodC throws a checked IOException. Show two options: (1) each method declares throws, propagating to main, or (2) methodB catches and wraps it. Compare both approaches.
hints: Option 1: add 'throws IOException' to methodB and methodA signatures.
Option 2: methodB catches IOException and throws new RuntimeException("msg", e).

solution.explanation: When a method calls code that declares throws CheckedException, it must either handle it (try-catch) or propagate it by also declaring throws CheckedException. Option 1 (propagation) is suitable when every layer in the chain cares about the specific exception type — for example, a CLI tool that handles IO differently from network errors. Option 2 (wrapping at the boundary) is the better choice when lower layers use implementation details (like JDBC SQLExceptions or file IOExceptions) that should not leak into higher-level APIs — it translates the vocabulary and avoids coupling callers to infrastructure details. Always preserve the original cause when wrapping so root-cause debugging remains possible.
